stances.claim: The SC's Bagumbayan v Comelec (March 8, 2016, 14-0, J Leonen ponente) properly ordered the Comelec to implement the Voter-Verified Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) for the May polls -- and after oral argument on March 17, the Court speedily denied the Comelec's MR with finality, again unanimously 13-0, rejecting the Comelec's claims that VVPAT was unnecessary, would delay casting, or required a 2-week election postponement to May 23 for source-code reconfiguration.

Under RA 9369 (authored by former Senator Richard Gordon, the Bagumbayan petitioner leader), the VVPAT lets voters 'verify if the choices on the paper record (or receipt spewed out by the VCM) match the choices that he or she actually made [on] the ballot' -- and the VCM (a 'paper-based automated system' 'seven times faster and more powerful than the PCOS') is allegedly capable of producing the VVPAT in two forms (printed receipt + touch screen).

The Comelec's counter-arguments -- (a) receipts enable vote-buying as proof of vote, (b) 5-7 hour casting delay, (c) paper receipt is 'surplusage' beyond paper ballot + ballot image + storage media cards + on-screen verification -- fail because the law is clear: 'the paper ballots cannot substitute for the voter's receipt'; 'voter verified' modifies 'paper audit trail' such that the voter himself or herself must verify; the paper ballot prevents fraud but doesn't provide voter security that the machine correctly recorded the vote; and on-screen verification 'is not the VVPAT because it is not paper-based.'

To prevent vote-buying via receipts, they should be 'deposited in a separate ballot box and not taken out of the precinct' -- and despite some casting delay, the VCMs can print simple receipts without reconfiguring source code, with additional security features (precinct/ballot numbers) reserved for future elections; the 2016 elections need not be postponed, and 'the poll body has no power to postpone the elections.'

Beyond VVPAT, three additional electoral reforms 'were not addressed adequately by past Comelec officials': (1) proclaim winners only after complete, correct, credible COC count -- in 2013, senatorial candidates were proclaimed based on the 'group canvass report' even though only 72 of 304 COCs had been duly canvassed; (2) allow thorough review of the source code, which is deposited in the BSP vault but was not reviewed prior to deposit; (3) implement random manual audit strictly in accordance with law.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban analyzes Bagumbayan v Comelec (March 8, 2016, written by Justice Marvic M. V. F. Leonen) in which the Supreme Court voting 14-0 ordered the Commission on Elections to implement the Voter-Verified Paper Audit Trail or VVPAT (say 'vivi pat' for easy recall) in the May polls. Comelec immediately filed a motion for reconsideration arguing that the VVPAT was unnecessary, would delay ballot casting, and might force a two-week postponement of elections (May 9 → May 23) for source-code reconfiguration. After oral argument on March 17, the Court speedily denied the motion with finality, again unanimously 13-0. The 2010 and 2013 elections used the now-famous (or 'infamous'?) precinct count optical scan (PCOS) machines; for 2016, Comelec opted for the vote-counting machine (VCM), a 'paper-based automated system' 'seven times faster and more powerful than the PCOS' with updated processor, memory, and security features. The VCM is allegedly capable of producing the VVPAT in two forms -- a printed receipt and a touch screen -- both showing the votes counted, and providing RA 9369's electoral safeguards: (a) voter verified paper audit trail, (b) system auditability with supporting documentation for verifying correctness, and (c) system allowing voter to find out whether the machine has registered his choice. Bagumbayan, led by former Senator Richard Gordon (RA 9369's author), argued that VVPAT lets voters verify their receipt matches actual choices on the ballot, with electronic results auditable and verifiable via paper records. Comelec countered that (a) receipts could be used for vote-buying as proof of vote, (b) voting would be delayed by 5-7 hours, and (c) paper receipt is 'surplusage' since the VCM provides numerous audit trails: paper ballot, ballot image, storage media cards, and on-screen verification; the receipt is required only in a 'direct recording electronic election system' where voters input on a monitor without shading a paper ballot, so with VCM's paper ballot, a printed receipt is unnecessary. The Court held the 'law is clear... The paper ballots cannot substitute for the voter's receipt.' The phrase 'voter verified' modifies 'paper audit trail,' meaning the voter himself or herself must verify the paper trail -- paper ballots are a form of paper audit trail but not voter-verified, and while the paper ballot assists in preventing fraud, 'it does not provide the security to the voter that the machine has correctly recorded his or her vote.' On-screen verification 'is not the VVPAT because it is not paper-based,' and digitized ballot images alone cannot fulfill VVPAT because verification 'at minimum should be paper-based.' To prevent vote-buying, receipts 'should be deposited in a separate ballot box and not taken out of the precinct.' The Court was convinced VCMs can print simple receipts without source-code reconfiguration, with additional security features (precinct/ballot numbers) for future elections; 2016 elections need not be postponed, and 'the poll body has no power to postpone the elections.' Beyond VVPAT, CJ proposes three additional reforms: (1) proclaim winners only after complete, correct, credible COC count -- in 2013 senatorial candidates were proclaimed based on the so-called 'group canvass report' even though only 72 of 304 COCs had been duly canvassed (see CJ columns May 19 + 26, 2013); (2) allow thorough source-code review (it has been deposited in the Bangko Sentral vault, but questions linger because it was not reviewed before deposit); (3) implement random manual audit strictly in accordance with law.
